summary: Specifies a leasequery exchange for DHCPv6, so lease information about clients can be obtained from a server. It defines the data that can be retrieved and the behavior of requestors and servers. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Asking the address handout desk who currently has which address.

questions: what is a dhcpv6 lease query by client id
what are dhcpv6 leasequery status codes
subtitle: A read-only DHCPv6 message pair that lets a router or other requestor ask a server who holds which address or prefix.

tldr.problem: DHCPv6 servers keep authoritative lease information about addresses and delegated prefixes, but devices such as broadband access concentrators had no standard way to retrieve it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5007 adds two messages, LEASEQUERY and LEASEQUERY-REPLY, plus new options. A requestor asks by IPv6 address or by client identifier (DUID), and the server returns the matching client data without changing any state.
tldr.outcome: It gives access concentrators a lightweight way to refresh client and binding information, which supports forwarding and source address verification. Servers are expected to restrict who can ask and what they can learn.

today: RFC 5007 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Ask a DHCPv6 Server
sections.content:
RFC 3315 defines DHCPv6, which hands out IPv6 addresses and configuration data, and RFC 3633 adds delegation of IPv6 prefixes. As with DHCPv4, DHCPv6 servers keep authoritative information about their operations, including lease information for addresses and delegated prefixes.

Many IPv6 deployments, particularly broadband ones, want to retrieve that data programmatically. Edge devices can use it for access control. The capability is called leasequery, and it parallels the DHCPv4 leasequery in RFC 4388. Differences come from IPv4 versus IPv6; for example, Neighbor Discovery replaces ARP.
sections.eli5: A server remembers who got which address. Leasequery is a polite way for another device to ask the server to look it up.

sections.title: Protocol Overview and Query Types
sections.content:
The goal is to let processes and devices read information from a DHCPv6 server in a lightweight way, especially those that already interpret DHCPv6 messages. A LEASEQUERY message is a query only: it does not change the state of the address, the prefix or the binding information.

The RFC specifies the on-demand query, which asks for just what an immediate need requires. For an access concentrator, that is typically a packet arriving for an address whose client information it must refresh, so the request is by address. This has limits with prefix delegation, because no traffic may arrive if the concentrator cannot inject routing information, such as after a reboot. An anticipatory query, which would rebuild a whole data store early, is not specified and is left as future work.

Two query types exist:

  • Query by IPv6 address: returns the bindings for the client bound to that address, or delegated a prefix containing it.
  • Query by Client Identifier (DUID): returns the bindings for a specific client on a specific link, or the list of links where the client has bindings.
sections.eli5: You can ask the desk two kinds of questions: 'Who has this room number?' or 'Which rooms does this person have?' Asking never changes who has what.

sections.title: New Messages and Options
sections.content:
Both messages use the DHCPv6 client/server message format. LEASEQUERY has message code 14 and LEASEQUERY-REPLY has code 15.

Five options carry the data:

  • OPTION_LQ_QUERY (44) appears only in a query. It holds a query-type, a link-address (a global address identifying the link, or 0::0 if unspecified) and query-options. Its option-len is 17 plus the length of the query-options.
  • OPTION_CLIENT_DATA (45) wraps the data for one client on one link in a reply. It includes OPTION_CLIENTID, OPTION_IAADDR, OPTION_IAPREFIX and OPTION_CLT_TIME, plus any requested options.
  • OPTION_CLT_TIME (46) is four bytes giving the seconds since the server last communicated with the client on that link.
  • OPTION_LQ_RELAY_DATA (47) returns the last complete relayed message, with the client's own OPTION_RELAY_MSG removed, plus the peer-address of the relay agent. It SHOULD only be returned if requested.
  • OPTION_LQ_CLIENT_LINK (48) lists the links where a client has bindings; its length must be a multiple of 16.

QUERY_BY_ADDRESS (1) requires an OPTION_IAADDR in the query-options. QUERY_BY_CLIENTID (2) requires an OPTION_CLIENTID. The query-options MAY also carry an OPTION_ORO listing which client options the requestor wants back.
sections.eli5: The question and the answer come in labelled envelopes. One envelope holds the question, another holds the facts about one person, and another says when they were last seen.

sections.title: Status Codes and Message Validation
sections.content:
Four new status codes report problems: UnknownQueryType (7), MalformedQuery (8), NotConfigured (9) and NotAllowed (10).

Validation rules keep the exchange tidy. Requestors and clients MUST discard any LEASEQUERY they receive. A server MUST discard a LEASEQUERY that lacks an OPTION_CLIENTID or an OPTION_LQ_QUERY, or whose OPTION_SERVERID does not match its own. A requestor MUST discard a reply that lacks OPTION_SERVERID, whose OPTION_CLIENTID does not match its own DUID, or whose transaction-id does not match the request. Servers and relay agents on port 547 MUST discard any LEASEQUERY-REPLY.
sections.eli5: If a question is garbled, in the wrong place or from the wrong person, it gets thrown away. Real problems get a short coded answer saying what went wrong.

sections.title: Requestor Behavior
sections.content:
The requestor sets the message type to LEASEQUERY, generates a transaction ID, MUST include an OPTION_CLIENTID to identify itself and MUST include an OPTION_LQ_QUERY. It SHOULD include an OPTION_SERVERID if it is not unicasting but wants an answer from one specific server.

It may be configured with a list of destination addresses, including unicast addresses or the All_DHCP_Servers multicast address, which it MAY use by default. It retransmits as described in RFC 3315 using the parameters: initial timeout LQ_TIMEOUT of 1 second, maximum timeout LQ_MAX_RT of 10 seconds and maximum retries LQ_MAX_RC of 5. If the exchange fails, local policy decides, for example trying another server.

A successful reply has one of three forms: it contains an OPTION_CLIENT_DATA (the requestor updates its database, and SHOULD silently discard the data if it has no OPTION_CLT_TIME); it contains an OPTION_CLIENT_LINK, so the requestor must repeat the query for each listed link; or it contains neither, meaning the server has no bindings for the client.

If several servers answer, disjoint data (different types or values) SHOULD be merged. For conflicting data about the same address, the requestor SHOULD use OPTION_CLT_TIME and accept the most recent.
sections.eli5: The asker sends its question to one or more desks and tries again a few times if nobody answers. If two desks disagree, it trusts the one that heard from the person most recently.

sections.title: Server Behavior
sections.content:
On a valid LEASEQUERY, the server finds the client, collects its data and returns a LEASEQUERY-REPLY with the same transaction ID. A query cannot be used to assign, release or otherwise modify bindings. An unknown query-type earns UnknownQueryType, and missing required options earn MalformedQuery. A server that restricts requestors MAY either discard the query or answer with NotAllowed.

A non-zero link-address MUST be used to find the link. For an address query with 0::0, the server uses the address itself. If it cannot find the link, it SHOULD return NotConfigured. For a client-ID query with 0::0, the server MUST search all of its links. If the client is on one link, its data SHOULD be returned in an OPTION_CLIENT_DATA; if on several, the server MUST return the list in OPTION_CLIENT_LINK and MUST NOT return any client data.

Each OPTION_CLIENT_DATA MUST contain the client ID, at least one of OPTION_IAADDR or OPTION_IAPREFIX, and OPTION_CLT_TIME. Servers SHOULD be configurable with a list of sensitive options that are never returned, even when requested.
sections.eli5: The desk looks up the person, writes down what it knows and sends it back. It may never change the records because someone asked, and it can keep some secrets off the list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Access concentrators are expected to be common requestors. Using DHCPv6 gleaning refreshed with leasequery helps them forward traffic correctly, verify IPv6 source addresses and encrypt traffic for the intended access modem.

Where the requestor is an access concentrator, the IPsec-based security in Section 21.1 of RFC 3315 SHOULD be used; other requestors are essentially DHCPv6 clients and can use DHCPv6 authentication. Trusted relay agents could relay queries from untrusted sources, so this SHOULD be prevented at least at perimeter relay agents, and servers MAY discard relayed queries or restrict relay chaining. Servers SHOULD be able to restrict the information returned even to trusted requestors.

To limit denial-of-service risk, access concentrators SHOULD minimize queries, using negative caching and address restrictions. The RFC also advises rate limiting and notes that a malicious server could feed an access concentrator wrong lease information, which IPsec helps prevent.
sections.eli5: Only trusted helpers should be allowed to ask the desk questions, and they should not ask too often. Otherwise a troublemaker could jam the desk or hand out fake answers.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned the two new DHCPv6 message types, the five new option codes (OPTION_LQ_QUERY, OPTION_CLIENT_DATA, OPTION_CLT_TIME, OPTION_LQ_RELAY_DATA and OPTION_LQ_CLIENT_LINK) and the four new status codes in the DHCPv6 parameters registry.

IANA also created a registry for OPTION_LQ_QUERY query-type codes with the initial entries QUERY_BY_ADDRESS (1) and QUERY_BY_CLIENTID (2). New query types are assigned through Standards Action.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers was updated so everyone uses the same number for each new message and option.

messages.label: LEASEQUERY (14)
messages.note: Carries OPTION_LQ_QUERY: query by address or by client ID.

messages.label: LEASEQUERY-REPLY (15)
messages.note: Carries OPTION_CLIENT_DATA, OPTION_CLIENT_LINK or a status code.

items.label: OPTION_LQ_QUERY
items.desc: Query type, link-address and query-options; used only in LEASEQUERY.

items.label: OPTION_CLIENT_DATA
items.desc: Encapsulates the data for one client on one link.

items.label: OPTION_CLT_TIME
items.desc: Seconds since the server last communicated with the client.

items.label: OPTION_LQ_RELAY_DATA
items.desc: Last relayed message and relay agent peer-address.

items.label: OPTION_LQ_CLIENT_LINK
items.desc: Links on which the client has bindings.

items.label: UnknownQueryType
items.desc: The query-type is unknown to or not supported by the server.

items.label: MalformedQuery
items.desc: The query is not valid, for example a required query-option is missing.

items.label: NotConfigured
items.desc: The server does not have the target address or link in its configuration.

items.label: NotAllowed
items.desc: The server does not allow the requestor to issue this LEASEQUERY.
